File: docs/BENCHMARKS_AB_CASE_STUDY.md 1 | # 📄 Empirical Evaluation of Hybrid Multi-Tier AI Routing in Autonomous Coding Agents 2 | ## A Comparative A/B Case Study on Cost Optimization, Quality Preservation, and Reasoning Fidelity 3 | 4 | **Author:** [@dixieflatline76](https://github.com/dixieflatline76) · [spicebox.dev/nacho-flow](https://spicebox.dev/nacho-flow/) 5 | **Date:** August 2026 6 | **Document Classification:** Technical Whitepaper & Empirical Benchmark Report 7 | **Document Version:** `1.0.0` (Official Release, Aligned with Nacho Flow `v0.6.0`) 8 | 9 | --- 10 | 11 | ## 🔬 Executive Summary 12 | 13 | Autonomous AI coding agents (such as **Roo Code**, **Cline**, **Cursor**, and **Aider**) operate via iterative feedback loops where accumulated conversational history, project file maps, terminal outputs, and diagnostics are re-transmitted on every single turn. This architectural pattern induces a severe **"Context Snowball"**, causing routine turn costs (e.g., inspecting a log, checking a syntax definition, or executing `git status`) to cost upwards of $2.00–$3.00 per prompt at frontier cloud rates. 14 | 15 | This whitepaper presents an empirical, head-to-head A/B case study evaluating **Nacho Flow**—a high-performance, deterministic semantic AI gateway built in pure Go. We tasked Roo Code with implementing a non-trivial, multi-file software engineering feature in a TypeScript/VS Code extension repository under two hybrid routing configurations: 16 | 1. **Run A (Cost-Optimized Hybrid)**: Local GPU offload (`gemma4:12b-it-qat` on AMD ROCm) + Cloud Fast Coder (`qwen/qwen3-coder`). 17 | 2. **Run B (Reasoning-Optimized Hybrid)**: Local GPU offload (`gemma4:12b-it-qat` on AMD ROCm) + Cloud Frontier Reasoning (`google/gemini-3.7-flash` with Extended Thinking). 18 | 19 | Both runs were benchmarked against a **Direct Frontier Cloud Baseline** (`anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet` at standard API pricing). 20 | 21 | ### Key Empirical Findings: 22 | * **The Hybrid Architecture Slashes Cloud Spend by 87%–92%**: Even the "expensive" Gemini Extended Thinking run achieved an **86.93% cost reduction** ($0.7604 total spend vs. $5.8185 Sonnet baseline), while Run A achieved a **91.82% cost reduction** ($0.2473 spend). 23 | * **Local GPUs Absorbed High-Frequency Reads at $0.00**: Over 90,000 to 216,000 background context tokens were offloaded to the local AMD Radeon GPU across routine file read and grep turns with zero API spend. 24 | * **The Hidden Finding: Failure Cost & Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)**: While Run A was ~51¢ cheaper in raw token spend, it failed the feature implementation due to brittle YAML parsing and circular mock tests, necessitating human engineering intervention ($15.00 based on 15 minutes of recovery @ $60/hr). Run B succeeded on the first pass with zero rework. **The cheaper model was significantly more expensive when factoring in failure recovery.** 25 | 26 | --- 27 | 28 | ## 1. Introduction & The Economics of Agentic Workflows 29 | 30 | ### 1.1 The Context Snowball Trap 31 | Unlike single-turn conversational chatbots, autonomous coding agents maintain persistent multi-turn execution loops. To maintain situational awareness across a multi-file workspace, the agent harness re-transmits the entire transcript on each turn. 32 | 33 | ```mermaid 34 | flowchart LR 35 | Turn1["Turn 1: 2,500 Tokens
($0.007)"] --> Turn5["Turn 5: 18,000 Tokens
($0.054)"] 36 | Turn5 --> Turn15["Turn 15: 45,000 Tokens
($0.135)"] 37 | Turn15 --> Turn30["Turn 30: 110,000 Tokens
($0.330/turn!)"] 38 | ``` 39 | 40 | By Turn 20, an agent asking for a 2-line typo fix re-submits over 60,000 tokens of background context. Across a typical 50-turn feature implementation, token consumption frequently exceeds 2.5 million tokens, resulting in direct cloud bills of **$12.00 to $25.00 per single developer task**. 41 | 42 | ### 1.2 The Dilemma: Pure Local vs. Pure Cloud 43 | - **Pure Local Routing ($0.00)**: Running 100% on local hardware (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) eliminates API costs. However, local open-weight models (7B–14B parameters) suffer from **context dilution**, failing to adhere to complex JSON tool call schemas or correctly synthesize multi-file state machines once context exceeds 16k–24k tokens. 44 | - **Pure Cloud Routing ($$$$)**: Routing 100% of turns to Claude Sonnet or GPT-4o ensures high reasoning fidelity but results in massive economic inefficiency, paying frontier rates for trivial file searches and linter reads. 45 | 46 | ### 1.3 The Hybrid Edge Gateway Hypothesis 47 | A deterministic, low-latency edge gateway can evaluate incoming prompt context in real-time ($< 0.2\text{ms}$), routing early exploration, file inspections, and routine unit tests to workstation GPUs for **$0.00**, while automatically escalating to frontier cloud models only when prompt tokens accumulate, complex keywords appear, or local retries indicate friction. 48 | 49 | ### 1.4 The Hidden Cost: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) & Failure Recovery 50 | Industry analysis overwhelmingly fixates on raw cost-per-million-tokens.   6 | 
  7 | ## 1. Development Prerequisites
  8 | 
  9 | - **Go**: Version `1.22+` (supports `slog`, generic channels, and `atomic.Pointer`).

 15 | ## 2. Project Layout
 16 |

 35 | │   ├── server/             # HTTP reverse proxy, delayed header validator, stream normalizer (reasoning -> think), deals API

 51 | ## 3. Makefile Command Reference & Key Targets

 55 | | Target | Command Executed | Description & When to Use |

 57 | | **`make check`** | `fmt vet sec test-race` | **Primary local gate**: Run before every commit or PR. |
 58 | | **`make build`** | `go build ... -o bin/nacho-flow` | Compiles optimized local binary with embedded version. |
 59 | | **`make fmt`** | `gofmt -s -w .` | Simplifies and formats all Go source files. |
 60 | | **`make vet`** | `go vet ./...` | Analyzes code for potential correctness and bug patterns. |
 61 | | **`make lint`** | `golangci-lint run ./...` | Runs configured linter suite (`.golangci.yml`). |
 62 | | **`make sec`** | `gosec -exclude=G706 ./...` | Runs AST security analysis for CWE vulnerabilities. |
 63 | | **`make test`** | `go test -v ./...` | Runs standard unit tests across all packages. |
 64 | | **`make test-race`** | `go test -v -race -count=1 ./...` | Runs test suite with Go's race detector active. |
 65 | | **`make test-cover`**| `go test -coverprofile=...` | Generates interactive HTML test coverage report. |

 70 | | **`make bump-minor`**| `version_bump -type=minor` | Bumps minor version (e.g. `0.2.0` $\rightarrow$ `0.3.0`) & tags git. |
 71 | | **`make bump-major`**| `version_bump -type=major` | Bumps major version (e.g. `0.2.0` $\rightarrow$ `1.0.0`) & tags git. |
 72 | | **`make build-all`** | Multiple `GOOS`/`GOARCH` builds | Compiles binaries for Windows, Linux, and macOS (amd64/arm64). |

 78 | ## 4. Building & Running Locally

 90 | ## 5. Quality Assurance, Security & Testing
 91 | 
 92 | Nacho Flow follows strict **Test-Driven Development (TDD)** and quality standards:
 93 | - **TDD Workflow**: Write failing tests first (`Red`), implement minimal clean code (`Green`), and refactor.
 94 | - **Coverage Gate**: Every individual package must maintain $\ge 95\%$ statement coverage (repository target $\ge 96\%$).
 95 | - **Zero Anti-Patterns**: Lock-free atomic synchronization on hot paths (`sync/atomic.Pointer`), zero detached background goroutine leaks (lazy TTL eviction), and zero external dependencies.
 96 | 
 97 | ```bash
 98 | # Run all-in-one quality gate (fmt, vet, gosec, race tests)
 99 | make check
100 | 
101 | # Run AST security vulnerability analysis (matching Spice standards)
102 | make sec
103 | 
104 | # Run golangci-lint suite
105 | make lint
106 | 
107 | # Run all unit and integration tests with race detector
108 | make test-race
109 | # or: go test -count=1 -v -race ./...
110 | 
111 | # Generate HTML code coverage report
112 | make test-cover
113 | 
114 | # Check per-package test coverage
115 | go test -cover ./pkg/...
116 | 
117 | # Run advisory route tuner
118 | make tune
119 | ```

123 | ## 6. Benchmarking & Load Testing
124 | 
125 | Nacho Flow includes both standard Go micro-benchmarks (`testing.B`) and a dedicated high-throughput A/B load test CLI:
126 | 
127 | ### 6.1 End-to-End Proxy Pipeline Benchmark

148 | ## 7. Extending the Multi-Model Tool Normalizer (`pkg/router/tool_normalizer.go`)
149 | 
150 | When adding support for a new open-source LLM format family:
151 | 
152 | 1. **Add Token Signature to the Fast Pre-Filter**:
153 |    In `hasCandidateToolTokens`, add the unique opening marker bytes (e.g. `[CUSTOM_CALL]`). If none match, non-tool prompts bail out in 23.5ns with zero allocations.
154 | 2. **Implement Lexical Extraction**:
155 |    Use `extractBalancedJSON` to balance opening and closing `{}` or `[]` brackets without regex truncation.
156 | 3. **Add Comprehensive Test Case**:
157 |    Add a test case in `pkg/router/tool_normalizer_test.go` verifying:
158 |    - Tool name and arguments parsed correctly.
159 |    - Arguments formatted as stringified JSON.
160 |    - Cleaned text stripped of markers while preserving reasoning `<think>` tags.
161 |    - Add a corresponding `BenchmarkNormalize_<Format>` micro-benchmark.
162 | 
163 | ---
164 | 
165 | ## 8. Extending Nacho Flow: Adding a Custom Provider Plugin
166 | 
167 | To add a specialized provider plugin:
168 | 
169 | 1. **Implement Capability Interfaces (`pkg/provider/interfaces.go`)**:
170 |    ```go
171 |    package myprovider
172 | 
173 |    import "context"
174 | 
175 |    type MyCloudProvider struct {
176 |        id     string
177 |        apiKey string
178 |    }
179 | 
180 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) ID() string      { return "my_cloud" }
181 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) Name() string    { return "My Cloud Enterprise" }
182 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) BaseURL() string { return "https://api.mycloud.com/v1" }
183 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) IsLocal() bool   { return false }
184 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) GetAPIKey() string { return p.apiKey }
185 |    func (p *MyCloudProvider) GetHeaders() map[string]string {
186 |        return map[string]string{"X-Organization": "corp"}
187 |    }
188 |    ```
189 | 
190 | 2. **Register in the Registry**:
191 |    ```go
192 |    registry.Register(&MyCloudProvider{id: "my_cloud", apiKey: key})
193 |    ```
194 | 
195 | ---
196 | 
197 | ## 9. Release & CI/CD Pipeline
198 | 
199 | Nacho Flow uses a 2-stage release lifecycle in GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`):
200 | 
201 | 1. **Stage 1: Prerelease Build & Artifact Upload (`publish-release`)**:
202 |    - Triggered when a Release is **published as a Pre-release** (or Draft published as Pre-release).
203 |    - Cross-compiles Linux (`amd64`, `arm64`), macOS (`amd64`, `arm64`), and Windows (`amd64`).
204 |    - Azure Trusted Signing signs the Windows AMD64 executable.
205 |    - Uploads all compiled binaries and `checksums.txt` to the release assets.
206 | 
207 | 2. **Stage 2: Verification & Promotion to Latest (`distribute-release`)**:
208 |    - Test the pre-release binaries.
209 |    - Once verified, edit the release on GitHub and **uncheck "Set as a pre-release"** (promoting to Latest Release).
210 |    - The `distribute-release` job triggers, updating the Homebrew Tap formula and pushing WinGet package manifests to the `winget-pkgs` fork.
211 |

231 | * **Concurrency Guarantee**: **0 data races** under `go test -race ./...`.

 17 | ## 1. How the Evaluation Pipeline Works
 18 | 
 19 | When an agent (Roo Code, Cline, Aider, Cursor) sends a prompt turn, Nacho Flow evaluates your configured tiers sequentially from **top to bottom** (*First Match Wins*):
 20 | 
 21 | ```mermaid
 22 | flowchart TD
 23 |     Req["Incoming Prompt Turn"] --> Context["Classifier Extracts: Tokens, HasImages, HasTools, Keywords"]
 24 |     Context --> Tier1{"Tier 1 Expression Match?"}
 25 |     Tier1 -->|True| Route1["Route to Tier 1 Target"]
 26 |     Tier1 -->|False| Tier2{"Tier 2 Expression Match?"}
 27 |     Tier2 -->|True| Route2["Route to Tier 2 Target"]
 28 |     Tier2 -->|False| TierN{"Tier N Expression Match?"}
 29 |     TierN -->|True| RouteN["Route to Tier N Target"]
 30 |     TierN -->|False| Default["Route to Default Tier"]
 31 | ```
 32 |

 35 | ## 2. Available Context Variables & Tier Properties
 36 | 
 37 | ### Variables in `when` Expressions:
 38 | | Variable | Type | Description | Example Condition |
 39 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
 40 | | `Tokens` | `int` | Real-time adaptive estimated token count across all prompt messages | `Tokens < 16000` |
 41 | | `HasImages` | `bool` | `true` if any message contains screenshots or image URLs | `HasImages == true` |
 42 | | `HasTools` | `bool` | `true` if function/tool definitions or active tool calls are present | `HasTools == true` |
 43 | | `Keywords` | `[]string` | Code keywords detected **strictly in the latest user prompt** | `any(Keywords, { # in ['deadlock', 'mutex'] })` |
 44 | | `Retries` | `int` | Number of consecutive prompt retries in current session (sliding 5m TTL) | `Retries < 2` |
 45 | | `IsRetry` | `bool` | `true` if this prompt is a retry of a previous failure | `!IsRetry` |
 46 | | `Model` | `string` | The requested model ID sent by the client (e.g. `nacho-hybrid`) | `Model == 'nacho-coder'` |
 47 | 
 48 | ### Tier Properties:
 49 | - `max_context` (`int`): Optional. Upper bound of the model's context window (e.g. `16384`, `32768`). If `Tokens > max_context`, Nacho Flow immediately skips this tier with zero expression overhead.
 50 | - `strip_images` (`bool`): If `true`, strips raw base64 image strings from older conversation turns to prevent 400 errors on text-only models.
 51 | - `reasoning_effort` (`string`): Passes `"low"`, `"medium"`, or `"high"` to supported reasoning providers.

 55 | ## 3. Recommended Tier Ordering Strategy

 59 | ```text

 61 | [2. Multimodal Vision (Images)]    --> Route to Gemini Flash / Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Vision Encoders)
 62 | [3. Active Tool Calls]             --> Route to Cloud Fast Coder (High Tool Adherence)
 63 | [4. Routine Local Coding (< 16k)]  --> Route to Local GPU (Ollama/vLLM) ($0.00 / 100% Free)
 64 | [5. Retry Escalation (Retries>=2)] --> Route to Cloud Provider (Breaks Local Failure Loops)
 65 | [6. Large Context Overflow (>= 16k)]-> Route to Cheap Cloud Fast (e.g. Qwen 3 Coder / DeepSeek)
 66 | [Default Fallback]                 --> Reliable Cloud Fallback

 86 | | Pattern | `when` Condition | Purpose |

 88 | | **1. Standard Local Workhorse** | `Tokens < 16000 && !HasImages && Retries < 2` | Routes routine iterative turns to GPU for $0.00, breaking on failures. |
 89 | | **2. Concurrency / Math Escapement** | `any(Keywords, { # in ['deadlock', 'mutex', 'concurrency', 'race'] })` | Instantly flags deep reasoning keywords to DeepSeek-R1 / o1. |
 90 | | **3. Vision Escapement** | `HasImages` | Routes screenshot turns to vision models (Gemini Flash / Claude Sonnet). |
 91 | | **4. Tool-Safety Boundary** | `!HasTools && Tokens < 12000` | Restricts local models to pure code generation without calling external tools. |
 92 | | **5. Cloud Recovery Overflow** | `Tokens >= 16000 || HasTools || Retries >= 2` | Catch-all for large context overflow, tool execution, or retry recovery. |

204 | ## 6. Autonomous Cost-Penalty Auto-Tuning (`nacho-flow tune`)
205 | 
206 | While manual rule crafting is powerful, human developers shouldn't have to guess where their local model begins to struggle. Nacho Flow features an autonomous **Cost-Penalty Auto-Tuner** that analyzes your real-world coding telemetry, detects model failure boundaries, and synthesizes optimal rules.
207 | 
208 | ### 6.1 The Mathematical Problem: The "Context Cliff"
209 | Local open-weight models (e.g. `qwen2.5-coder:14b`, `deepseek-coder:6.7b`) are remarkably capable on concise prompt turns ($< 8\text{k}\text{--}12\text{k}$ tokens). However, as conversation history snowballs, smaller models experience **attention dilution** and context degradation:
210 | 1. **The Hidden Cost of Local Failures**: While a local GPU turn costs **$0.00** in direct API spend, a defective response that hallucinates an edit or breaks a file forces the human developer to manually intervene, rollback, or re-prompt. This costs minutes of developer flow state (quantified as a **~$2.00 penalty** per wasted retry).
211 | 2. **The Cloud Alternative**: Escalating a 20k token turn to an economy cloud model (e.g. `qwen3-coder` or `deepseek-v3`) costs only **~$0.03**.
212 | 3. **The Objective Function**: The auto-tuner runs a grid-search sweep across historical turns to find the threshold $T$ and friction keywords that maximize total utility:
213 |    $$\text{Utility} = - \text{CloudDirectSpend} - (\text{LocalRetries} \times \text{RetryPenaltyUSD})$$
214 | 
215 | ---
216 | 
217 | ### 6.2 Step-by-Step Tuning Workflow
218 | 
219 | #### Step 1: Accumulate Natural Traffic
220 | Run Nacho Flow during your normal coding workflow for a few days (recommended: 50 to 500 prompt turns). Nacho Flow automatically appends structured turn telemetry to `logs/traffic.jsonl`:
221 | ```json

223 | ```
224 | 
225 | #### Step 2: Run the Advisory Analysis (Dry-Run)
226 | Analyze your historical traffic without modifying any files:
227 | ```bash
228 | nacho-flow tune
229 | ```
230 | 
231 | **Example Advisory Output**:
232 | ```text

234 | 🌮 NACHO FLOW ADVISORY TUNING REPORT
235 | ========================================================================================
236 | 
237 | 📊 Sample Size: 240 historical prompt turns evaluated
238 | 
239 | 🔍 FRICTION & BOTTLENECK SIGNALS DETECTED:
240 |   • Optimal Local Context Threshold: 24,000 tokens
241 |   • Multimodal Vision:              Clean (0% retry rate — enabled locally)
242 |   • Agentic Tool Calls:             Clean (0% retry rate — enabled locally)
243 |   • High-Friction Domain Keywords:  ['deadlock', 'kubernetes', 'migration'] (Spikes local retry probability)

261 | #### Step 3: Understand the Signals in the Report
262 | * **Optimal Local Context Threshold (e.g. `24,000 tokens`)**: The exact token boundary where keeping requests on your local GPU begins costing more in developer retries than the modest API cost of escalating to cloud (bounded by the model's `max_context`).
263 | * **Multimodal Vision & Tool Call Status**: Reports whether local image or tool execution experiences failure spikes. If $\sim 0\%$ failures are recorded, modalities remain enabled for local processing without adding `!HasImages` or `!HasTools`.
264 | * **High-Friction Keywords (e.g. `['deadlock', 'kubernetes']`)**: Domains where the local model exhibited an odds ratio $\ge 1.5\times$ baseline retry rate. Nacho Flow synthesizes an exclusion rule to route these specific concepts directly to cloud reasoning.
265 | * **Preserved Guardrails (e.g. `Retries < 2`)**: Existing user conditions and escalation guards are automatically preserved via AST parsing.

267 | #### Step 4: Apply Recommendations Automatically
268 | To update your `config.yaml` with the synthesized rule:

294 | ## 7. Manual Heuristic Tuning Tips (For Custom Power Rules)
295 | 
296 | If you prefer writing and refining your own rules by hand:
297 | 
298 | 1. **Check Live Financials First**: Run `curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/stats` or view `@nacho:status` in your chat prompt to see your current local vs cloud distribution. Aim for **70%–85% local turns** on typical coding tasks.
299 | 2. **Start with Conservative Token Bounds**: If your local GPU has 16GB VRAM running a 14B model, set `Tokens < 12000`. If running an 8B model, set `Tokens < 8000`.
300 | 3. **Always Include `Retries < 2` on Local Tiers**: This ensures that if a local model produces a broken response, the agent's second attempt automatically escalates to a cloud frontier model (e.g. Claude Sonnet 5 or DeepSeek-R1) instead of looping indefinitely on local hardware.
301 | 4. **Use `strip_images: true` on Text-Only Local Models**: If your agent sends a screenshot in Turn 1, Turn 10 doesn't need 40,000 tokens of raw base64 image data sent to a text-only local model. Setting `strip_images: true` removes legacy base64 strings while preserving the conversational text.

307 | ### Q: How do I know if my local GPU is actually processing turns?
308 | - **Response Headers**: Check the `x-nacho-router-tier` and `x-nacho-target-model` headers returned in your agent's HTTP responses.
309 | - **In-Prompt Directive**: Type `@nacho:status` directly into your chat prompt to see total tokens routed locally vs to cloud and dollars saved.
310 | - **CLI Log Output**: When running interactively, the daemon prints green routing log entries:
311 |   ```text
312 |   INFO Routing request tier="Local ROCm GPU" model=qwen2.5-coder:14b tokens=4,120 is_fallback=false
313 |   ```
314 | 
315 | ### Q: What happens if Ollama or my local GPU runs out of VRAM or crashes?
316 | - **Zero Broken Loops**: Nacho Flow's built-in **Circuit Breaker** detects the connection failure or defective empty response and immediately re-routes the prompt to your configured `default_tier` (Cloud Fallback) with **0ms dial delay**.
317 | - **Exception**: If you explicitly forced `@nacho:local` via a HotSauce directive, Nacho Flow respects your strict override and returns a zero-cost chat alert instead of billing your credit card.
318 | 
319 | ### Q: How do I test a new rule before putting it in production?
320 | - You can override any turn on-the-fly directly from your chat prompt using **🌶️ HotSauce Directives** (`@nacho:local`, `@nacho:cloud`, `@nacho:reasoning`, `@nacho:tier="..."`, `@nacho:model="..."`) without modifying `config.yaml`.

233 | ## 3. Writing Custom Routing Tiers (`expr` Rules)
234 | 
235 | For a complete guide with recipes on tuning token thresholds, keyword extraction, and reasoning parameters, check out the **[Rule & Tier Tuning Guide](TUNING_GUIDE.md)**.
236 | 
237 | ### Available Variables in `when` Expressions:
238 | | Variable | Type | Description | Example |
239 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
240 | | `Tokens` | `int` | Real-time adaptive estimated token count of entire prompt history | `Tokens < 16000` |
241 | | `HasImages` | `bool` | `true` if the request includes screenshots or image URLs | `HasImages == true` |
242 | | `HasTools` | `bool` | `true` if the request provides function/tool definitions | `HasTools == true` |
243 | | `Keywords` | `[]string` | Extracted code keywords scoped to the **latest user prompt** (`mutex`, `sql`, `refactor`) | `any(Keywords, { # in ['deadlock', 'mutex'] })` |
244 | | `Retries` | `int` | Number of consecutive prompt retries recorded in the current session (sliding 5m TTL) | `Retries < 2` |
245 | | `IsRetry` | `bool` | `true` if the current request is a retry of a previous failure | `!IsRetry` |
246 | | `Model` | `string` | The requested model ID sent by the client | `Model == 'nacho-hybrid'` |
247 | 
248 | ### Tier Configuration Options:
249 | | Property | Type | Description |
250 | | :--- | :--- | :--- |
251 | | `name` | `string` | Human-readable label for logs and `x-nacho-router-tier` header. |
252 | | `model` | `string` | Upstream model identifier to rewrite in the payload. |
253 | | `provider` | `string` | Target provider key configured in `providers`. |
254 | | `when` | `string` | `expr` boolean expression. |
255 | | `max_context` | `int` | *(Optional)* Model context window size limit. Automatically skips this tier if `Tokens > max_context`. |
256 | | `strip_images`| `bool` | *(Optional)* If `true`, strips base64 images from conversation history. |
257 | | `reasoning_effort` | `string` | *(Optional)* Passes `reasoning_effort` (`"low"`, `"medium"`, `"high"`) to supported reasoning endpoints. |
258 | 
259 | ### ⚠️ Critical Rule: Top-to-Bottom Precedence (First Match Wins)
260 | Nacho Flow evaluates tiers sequentially from **top to bottom**. The **first tier whose `when` condition evaluates to `true` is selected**.
261 | 
262 | * **Place Narrow & Specialized Tiers at the TOP:** High-complexity keyword matching (`Keywords`), multimodal vision (`HasImages`), and agent tool calls (`HasTools`) must be listed before broad catch-all rules.
263 | * **Place Broad & Free Local Tiers in the MIDDLE:** Rules like `Tokens < 16000 && !HasImages && Retries < 2` should sit below specialized tiers to prevent shadowing reasoning prompts.
264 | * **Fallback Tier at the BOTTOM:** The `default_tier` acts as the safety net if none of the above match, or if an upstream local provider is unavailable.
265 | 
266 | ### 🛡️ Autonomous Self-Healing & Fallback Patterns
267 | 
268 | 1. **Adaptive Token Estimator**:  
269 |    Code and JSON payloads have a significantly higher token density (~3.0–3.2 chars/token) than standard English prose (~4.0 chars/token). Nacho Flow uses a self-calibrating Exponential Moving Average ($\alpha = 0.2$) estimator seeded at 3.2 chars/token with lock-free atomic updates from upstream `usage.prompt_tokens` feedback.
270 | 2. **Keyword Signal Scoping**:  
271 |    Keyword extraction is strictly scoped to the **latest user prompt**. This prevents past turns in a 20-turn session from permanently locking routing into expensive reasoning models when the user transitions to routine edits.
272 | 3. **Retry-Based Auto-Escalation**:  
273 |    If a local model generates malformed code or hallucinates, coding agents retry. Nacho Flow tracks session retry counts (keyed by prompt prefix hash with sliding 5-min TTL) so routing expressions like `Retries < 2` automatically escalate the turn to cloud models, breaking failure loops.
274 | 4. **Local Provider Circuit Breaker**:  
275 |    Monitors local provider errors (connection refused, timeouts, 5xx). After consecutive failures, the circuit breaker opens for 20 seconds, fast-failing local attempts in 0ms and routing directly to cloud fallback without client-visible errors.
276 | 5. **Delayed Header / Quality Fallback**:  
277 |    For streaming SSE requests, Nacho Flow delays sending `200 OK` until peeking the first data chunk. If the local model returns empty choices or immediate `data: [DONE]`, Nacho Flow transparently cancels the local attempt and streams from the default fallback tier.
278 | 
279 | ### 🛠️ Universal Multi-Model Tool-Calling Normalizer
280 | Open-source models (e.g. Qwen 2.5, Mistral, Llama 3.1, Hermes) often return tool calls formatted inside markdown code fences or specialized XML tags rather than native OpenAI `tool_calls` structures.
281 | 
282 | Nacho Flow includes a **zero-alloc lexical bracket balancer** that automatically detects and converts 7 format families on the fly:
283 | 1. **Hermes / Nous / Qwen ChatML**: `<tool_call>{"name":"...","arguments":{...}}</tool_call>`
284 | 2. **Mistral / Mixtral**: `[TOOL_CALLS] [{"name":"...","arguments":{...}}]`
285 | 3. **Llama 3 Tags**: `<function=name>{"param":"value"}</function>`
286 | 4. **Llama 3.1 Python Calls**: `<|python_tag|>tool_name.call(param="value")`
287 | 5. **Claude XML Format**: `<function_calls><invoke name="..."><parameter name="...">...</parameter></invoke></function_calls>`
288 | 6. **ReAct / LangChain**: `Action: tool_name\nAction Input: {...}`
289 | 7. **DeepSeek-R1 & Qwen Reasoning**: Preserves `<think>...</think>`, `<|im_start|>think`, and `<thinking>` internal thoughts while extracting the embedded tool call block.
290 | 
291 | Nacho Flow converts all of these into standard OpenAI `tool_calls` arrays with stringified `function.arguments` JSON, enabling **flawless tool execution in Roo Code, Cline, Cursor, and Continue**.

664 | ## 9. 🌶️ HotSauce Directives (In-Prompt Routing & Meta Commands)
665 | 
666 | ### 🔥 Heat Seeker & 🌶️ HotSauce Directives
667 | 
668 | Two ways to optimize your routing costs:
669 | 
670 | - **Heat Seeker** runs autonomously in the background, continuously scanning 300+ models for underpriced capacity. When it finds a deal meeting your thresholds, it surfaces it as a one-click tier substitution.
671 | - **HotSauce Directives** let you manually override routing on any turn by adding `@nacho:local`, `@nacho:cloud`, or `@nacho:reasoning` to your prompt.
672 | 
673 | > **Together: Heat Seeker finds the fire. HotSauce lets you pour it on.**
674 | 
675 | ---
676 | 
677 | **HotSauce Directives** allow developers and autonomous coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Roo Code, Aider, OpenCode) to manually spice up prompt turns with instant routing overrides or inspect daemon metadata dynamically directly from conversational prompts using zero-cost `@nacho:` tags.
678 | 
679 | ### 🔥 Heat Levels (Routing Overrides)
680 | 
681 | Splash any HotSauce directive into your prompt to override automatic rule evaluation for a single turn:
682 | 
683 | | Directive | Heat Level | Behavior | Example |
684 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
685 | | `@nacho:local` | 🟢 **Mild** | Forces routing to your local GPU tier ($0.00 / Ollama / ROCm / CUDA). | `@nacho:local write a unit test for this function` |
686 | | `@nacho:cloud` | 🟡 **Medium** | Forces routing to your cloud workhorse / fallback tier. | `@nacho:cloud analyze this multi-file architecture` |
687 | | `@nacho:frontier` | 🟠 **Extra Hot** | Forces routing to your frontier cloud tier (Claude Sonnet 5 / GPT-4o). | `@nacho:frontier refactor this complex state machine` |
688 | | `@nacho:reasoning` | 🔥 **Inferno** | Forces routing to your deep reasoning tier (DeepSeek-R1 / o1). | `@nacho:reasoning prove why this algorithm is O(N log N)` |
689 | | `@nacho:tier="<Name>"` | 🌶️ **Custom** | Forces routing to a specific named tier from `config.yaml`. | `@nacho:tier="Tier 1: Local ROCm" quick fix` |
690 | | `@nacho:model="<ID>"` | 🌶️ **Chef's Special** | Directs request straight to a specific model ID across any configured provider. | `@nacho:model="deepseek/deepseek-r1" solve this concurrency race` |
691 | 
692 | #### Architectural Guarantees:
693 | 1. **Clean Upstream Forwarding**: All `@nacho:` tags are automatically stripped and whitespace is collapsed before the prompt reaches upstream LLMs. The model never sees the directive.
694 | 2. **Zero Proxy Regression**: Detection uses SIMD fast bailout (`strings.Contains`), taking `< 7 ns` and `0 bytes` heap allocation for standard prompts.
695 | 3. **Strict Circuit Alert (Fallback Bypass)**: If you force `@nacho:local` and your local GPU/Ollama instance is offline (Circuit Breaker: OPEN), Nacho Flow does **not** silently fall through to an expensive cloud model. Instead, it instantly returns an OpenAI wire-compliant zero-cost chat alert explaining that the local provider is down and how to resolve it.
696 | 
697 | ---
698 | 
699 | ### Zero-Cost Meta Commands
700 | 
701 | Meta directives are executed entirely in-process by the daemon and return instantly with **$0.00** LLM cost and **0 upstream tokens consumed**:
702 | 
703 | | Directive | Output | Description |
704 | | :--- | :--- | :--- |
705 | | `@nacho:help` | Markdown Quick-Start Guide | Displays all available HotSauce directives, heat levels, and active daemon version. |
706 | | `@nacho:tiers` | Active Tier Catalog | Lists all configured routing tiers, models, and providers currently loaded from `config.yaml`. |
707 | | `@nacho:status` | Daemon Telemetry & Health | Live uptime, circuit breaker states, token volume, and total dollars saved vs spent. |
708 | | `@nacho:deals` | Heat Seeker Spot Deals | Real-time spot market flash discounts and promotional pricing from pricing oracles. |
709 | 
710 | #### Client Compatibility & Anti-Abuse:
711 | - **Universal Wire Format**: Works seamlessly with streaming (`stream: true` SSE chunks) and non-streaming (`chat.completion` JSON) clients.
712 | - **Levenshtein Typo Matcher**: Unrecognized tags like `@nacho:helpp` or `@nacho:statuss` return an instant helper message: *"Did you mean `@nacho:help`?"*.
713 | - **Anti-Abuse Debounce**: Rapid repeated meta queries within 2 seconds receive a lightweight cached acknowledgment to prevent agent loops.

 96 | ## 4. 8-Format Multi-Model Tool Normalizer Pipeline
 97 | 
 98 | Local and open-weights models (e.g. Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral, Command-R) frequently emit tool calls as embedded text instead of standard OpenAI JSON schema. Nacho Flow intercepts and normalizes 8 distinct formats:
 99 | 
100 | 1. **Bare JSON**: Text responses containing raw JSON function call payloads.
101 | 2. **Markdown JSON Code Fences**: ` ```json\n{"name": "...", "arguments": {...}}\n``` `.
102 | 3. **Hermes / Claude XML Tags**: `<tool_call>\n{"name": "...", "arguments": {...}}\n</tool_call>`.
103 | 4. **Mistral Array Calls**: `[{"name": "...", "arguments": {...}}]`.
104 | 5. **DeepSeek-R1 Reasoning + Tool**: Extracts `<think>...</think>` into `reasoning_content` while promoting embedded tool invocations to standard `tool_calls`.
105 | 6. **Llama 3 Tool Syntax**: `<|python_tag|>` function call formats.
106 | 7. **Custom Function Objects**: `[CALL func_name(arg=val)]` patterns.
107 | 8. **Standard OpenAI Passthrough**: Verifies existing `tool_calls` structures.

 82 | 
 83 | ### 3.1 `GET /api/v1/info` — Daemon Discovery & Version Negotiation
 84 | * **Auth Required:** No (Public)
 85 | * **Purpose:** Called on extension startup to verify connectivity and negotiate capability flags.
 86 | 
 87 | #### Response (`200 OK`):

 91 |   "version": "0.6.0",
 92 |   "features": [

106 | ### 3.2 `GET /api/v1/events` — Real-Time SSE Telemetry Stream
107 | * **Auth Required:** Yes (`Bearer <token>`)
108 | * **Headers:** `Accept: text/event-stream`
109 | * **Purpose:** Establishes a long-lived Server-Sent Events stream. The extension connects to this on startup to receive real-time UI updates without polling.
110 | * **Keep-Alive:** The daemon sends a comment line (`: ping\n\n`) every 15 seconds to prevent proxy/socket disconnects.
111 | 
112 | #### Event Stream Format:
113 | ```http
114 | HTTP/1.1 200 OK
115 | Content-Type: text/event-stream
116 | Cache-Control: no-cache
117 | Connection: keep-alive
118 | Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
119 |

289 | ### 3.8 `PUT /api/v1/config` — Atomic Hot-Reload with Secret Merging & Dry Run
290 | * **Auth Required:** Yes
291 | * **Query Parameters:**
292 |   * `dry_run=true` *(optional)*: Validates syntax and test-compiles AST expressions without modifying runtime state or saving to disk.
293 | * **Payload:** Complete or partial JSON config matching the schema above.
294 | 
295 | #### Behavior:
296 | 1. **Secret Deep-Merge:** Any fields containing `***` (e.g. `"api_key": "sk-or-v1-***"`) automatically inherit the existing active secret from daemon memory.
297 | 2. **AST Pre-Compilation:** Compiles all `when` expressions against `contract.RequestContext`. If any syntax error occurs, immediately rejects with `400 Bad Request`.
298 | 3. **Atomic Swap & Rollback Watchdog:** Creates a timestamped `.bak` on disk, swaps memory pointers with zero dropped requests, and arms a 30s auto-rollback watchdog.
299 | 
300 | #### Success Response (`200 OK`):
301 | ```json
302 | {
303 |   "status": "ok",
304 |   "message": "Configuration validated and atomically hot-reloaded",
305 |   "backup_file": "config.yaml.bak.20260822T180500"
306 | }
307 | ```
308 | 
309 | #### Error Response (`400 Bad Request`):
310 | ```json
311 | {
312 |   "error": {
313 |     "type": "invalid_config",
314 |     "message": "failed to compile expr for tier 'Tier 1' (Tokens < 8000 && invalid_token): unknown name invalid_token"
315 |   }
316 | }
317 | ```

363 | ## 4. UI Component Architecture for Roo Code
364 | 
365 | Roo Code can build the extension progressively across 3 tiers:
366 | 
367 | ### Tier 1: Core MVP (Status Bar & Health Indicator)
368 | 1. **Status Bar Item (`StatusBarItem`):**
369 |    - Text: `$(pulse) Nacho: $3.85 saved (70% local)`
370 |    - Tooltip: Total requests, current active tier, daemon connection state.
371 |    - Click Action: Opens the Nacho Flow Dashboard Webview.
372 | 2. **Connection Health Watchdog:**
373 |    - Connects to `/api/v1/events` SSE.
374 |    - If SSE disconnects, shows `$(alert) Nacho: Offline` and attempts exponential backoff reconnection.
375 | 3. **Roo Code Integration Validator:**
376 |    - Detects if VS Code `settings.json` or Roo Code provider config points to `http://localhost:8000/v1`.
377 |    - 1-Click "Fix Roo Code Config" command.
378 | 
379 | ### Tier 2: Route History & Circuit Breakers Panel (Webview)
380 | 1. **Route History Table:**
381 |    - Rendered using VS Code Webview Toolkit or sleek modern CSS.
382 |    - Live appends incoming `route_completed` events from SSE.
383 |    - Badges: `Local (0ms/Free)`, `Cloud Coder ($)`, `Fallback (!)`.
384 | 2. **Circuit Breaker Status Cards:**
385 |    - Displays real-time status of Ollama & OpenRouter.
386 |    - Red badge if `Open` (tripped).
387 |    - "Reset Circuit" button firing `POST /api/v1/circuits/reset`.
388 | 
389 | ### Tier 3: Visual Config Editor & Auto-Tuning Panel
390 | 1. **Interactive Rule Editor:**
391 |    - Sliders for token thresholds (`tokens < 8000`).
392 |    - Toggles for `has_images`, `has_tools`.
393 |    - "Test Rule" button triggering `PUT /api/v1/config?dry_run=true`.
394 |    - "Apply Changes" button triggering live hot-reload.
395 | 2. **Tuning Advisor Card:**
396 |    - "Run Optimizer" button calling `POST /api/v1/tune`.
397 |    - Displays projected savings and recommended `when` expression with a 1-click "Apply Optimization" button.

======================================================
 🎓 Level 3: Recursion & Backtracking (The Tree Explorer)
======================================================

How do computers solve this? Classical Backtracking works like walking a maze:
1. Try placing a queen on the first safe square in Row 0.
2. Move to Row 1 and find a safe spot.
3. If you reach a row where NO squares are safe, you've hit a dead end!
4. You BACKTRACK (rewind), move the previous queen, and explore new branches.

======================================================
 🎓 Level 4: Heuristics & Local Search (Tackling N=1000!)
======================================================

Backtracking is great for small boards, but for N=1000, 2^1000 is more than atoms in the universe!
Instead, we use 'Min-Conflicts Local Search':
1. Place 1000 queens randomly (one per row).
2. Find any queen that is currently fighting with others.
3. Slide that queen to the column in its row that minimizes conflicts.
4. Repeat until 0 conflicts remain! This takes under 5 milliseconds in Go!

 65 | func (s *Simulator) Run() *SimulationResult {
 66 | 	// For better performance with large numbers of runs, we'll use goroutines

 68 | 	numWorkers := 4
 69 | 	runsPerWorker := s.Runs / numWorkers
 70 | 
 71 | 	var wg sync.WaitGroup
 72 | 	resultsChan := make(chan *SimulationResult, numWorkers)
 73 | 
 74 | 	startTime := time.Now()
 75 | 
 76 | 	// Launch worker goroutines
 77 | 	for i := 0; i < numWorkers; i++ {
 78 | 		wg.Add(1)
 79 | 		go func(workerID int) {
 80 | 			defer wg.Done()
 81 | 			workerResult := s.runWorker(runsPerWorker)
 82 | 			resultsChan <- workerResult
 83 | 		}(i)
 84 | 	}
 85 | 
 86 | 	// Close the results channel when all workers are done
 87 | 	go func() {
 88 | 		wg.Wait()
 89 | 		close(resultsChan)
 90 | 	}()
 91 | 
 92 | 	// Collect results from all workers
 93 | 	finalResult := &SimulationResult{}
 94 | 	for workerResult := range resultsChan {
 95 | 		finalResult.TotalHands += workerResult.TotalHands
 96 | 		finalResult.PlayerWins += workerResult.PlayerWins
 97 | 		finalResult.DealerWins += workerResult.DealerWins
 98 | 		finalResult.Pushes += workerResult.Pushes
 99 | 		finalResult.PlayerBlackjacks += workerResult.PlayerBlackjacks
100 | 		finalResult.NetProfit += workerResult.NetProfit
101 | 		finalResult.AvgBetSize += workerResult.AvgBetSize * float64(workerResult.TotalHands) // Weighted average
102 | 	}
103 |

106 | 		finalResult.AvgBetSize /= float64(finalResult.TotalHands)

111 | 	finalResult.ExpectedValue = finalResult.NetProfit / float64(finalResult.TotalHands)
112 | 	finalResult.HouseEdge = -finalResult.ExpectedValue / finalResult.AvgBetSize

// simulateSingleGame simulates a single hand and returns its resolved outcome
// along with the number of cards consumed from the shoe.
func (s *Simulator) simulateSingleGame(shoe *cards.Shoe, counter *oracle.CardCounter, rng *rand.Rand) (Outcome, int) {
	dealt := 0

	draw := func() cards.Card {
		c, err := shoe.DrawCard()
		if err != nil {
			return cards.Card{}
		}
		dealt++
		counter.UpdateCount(c)
		return c
	}

	playerHand := &game.Hand{
		Cards:  make([]cards.Card, 0, 2),
		Bet:    s.BaseBet,
		Active: true,
	}
	dealerHand := &game.Hand{Cards: make([]cards.Card, 0, 2)}

	playerHand.Cards = append(playerHand.Cards, draw())
	dealerHand.Cards = append(dealerHand.Cards, draw())
	playerHand.Cards = append(playerHand.Cards, draw())
	dealerHand.Cards = append(dealerHand.Cards, draw())

	playerHasBlackjack := s.isBlackjackHand(playerHand)
	dealerHasBlackjack := s.isBlackjackHand(dealerHand)
	playerHand.IsBlackjack = playerHasBlackjack
	dealerHand.IsBlackjack = dealerHasBlackjack

	// A natural on either side ends the hand immediately.
	if playerHasBlackjack || dealerHasBlackjack {
		return s.resolveOutcome(playerHand, dealerHand), dealt
	}

	advisor := oracle.NewStrategyAdvisor(s.RuleSet, counter)

	if s.UseBasicStrategy {
		playerHand = s.playPlayerTurn(playerHand, dealerHand.Cards[0], shoe, advisor, counter)
	} else {
		playerHand = s.playRandomPlayerTurn(playerHand, dealerHand.Cards[0], shoe)
	}

	// The dealer only draws if the player is still live; a busted player is
	// settled without the dealer completing the hand.
	if !playerHand.IsBusted {
		dealerHand = s.playDealerTurn(dealerHand, shoe, s.RuleSet)
	}

	return s.resolveOutcome(playerHand, dealerHand), dealt
}

// resolveOutcome compares a completed player hand against the dealer and
// converts the comparison into a signed profit figure.
func (s *Simulator) resolveOutcome(playerHand, dealerHand *game.Hand) Outcome {
	bet := playerHand.Bet
	out := Outcome{AmountBet: bet, IsBlackjack: playerHand.IsBlackjack}

	playerValue := s.getHandValue(playerHand.Cards)
	dealerValue := s.getHandValue(dealerHand.Cards)
	playerBusted := playerHand.IsBusted || playerValue > 21
	dealerBusted := dealerHand.IsBusted || dealerValue > 21

	payout := s.RuleSet.BlackjackPayout
	if payout <= 0 {
		payout = 1.5
	}

	switch {
	case playerHand.IsBlackjack && dealerHand.IsBlackjack:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "push", 0
	case playerHand.IsBlackjack:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "blackjack", bet*payout
	case dealerHand.IsBlackjack:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "lose", -bet
	case playerBusted:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "lose", -bet
	case dealerBusted:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "win", bet
	case playerValue > dealerValue:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "win", bet
	case playerValue < dealerValue:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "lose", -bet
	default:
		out.Result, out.NetProfit = "push", 0
	}

	return out
}

20 | func (b *BacktrackingSolver) Solve(n int) ([]models.Solution, error) {
21 | 	if n <= 0 {
22 | 		return nil, errors.New("n must be positive")
23 | 	}
24 | 	if n == 1 {
25 | 		return []models.Solution{
26 | 			{Queens: []models.Queen{{Row: 0, Col: 0}}},
27 | 		}, nil
28 | 	}
29 | 	if n >= 17 { // For large N, this algorithm becomes too slow. We'll suggest MinConflicts.

31 | 	}

34 | 	board := make([]int, n) // board[row] = col
35 | 
36 | 	// Use bitwise flags for efficient constraint tracking
37 | 	// cols: tracks which columns are occupied
38 | 	// diag1: tracks diagonals (top-left to bottom-right), identified by (row - col + n - 1)
39 | 	// diag2: tracks anti-diagonals (top-right to bottom-left), identified by (row + col)
40 | 	cols := 0
41 | 	diag1 := 0
42 | 	diag2 := 0
43 | 
44 | 	// Initialize the board with -1 (no queen placed)
45 | 	for i := range board {
46 | 		board[i] = -1
47 | 	}
48 |

50 | 
51 | 	return solutions, nil
52 | }

54 | // solveRecursive is the core recursive backtracking function.
55 | func (b *BacktrackingSolver) solveRecursive(row, n int, board []int, solutions *[]models.Solution, cols, diag1, diag2 *int) {
56 | 	if row == n {
57 | 		// Found a valid solution, convert board state to Solution struct
58 | 		sol := models.Solution{Queens: make([]models.Queen, n)}
59 | 		for r := 0; r < n; r++ {
60 | 			sol.Queens[r] = models.Queen{Row: r, Col: board[r]}
61 | 		}

63 | 		return
64 | 	}
65 |

67 | 		// Calculate bit positions for the current position
68 | 		colBit := 1 << col
69 | 		diag1Bit := 1 << (row - col + n - 1) // Shift to avoid negative indices
70 | 		diag2Bit := 1 << (row + col)
71 | 
72 | 		// Check if the position is under attack
73 | 		if (*cols&colBit) != 0 || (*diag1&diag1Bit) != 0 || (*diag2&diag2Bit) != 0 {

75 | 		}

80 | 		*diag1 |= diag1Bit
81 | 		*diag2 |= diag2Bit
82 |

85 | 
86 | 		// Backtrack: remove the queen and reset bits
87 | 		*cols &= ^colBit
88 | 		*diag1 &= ^diag1Bit
89 | 		*diag2 &= ^diag2Bit
90 | 	}
91 | }
